group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department late this morning after four days of gradually increasing shortness of breath, pleuritic discomfort just below the right scapula, and a cough that progressed from dry to producing scant rust-tinged sputum overnight; she also noted a recorded temperature no higher than 37.5 °C at home, chills while climbing the stairs to her bedroom, and fatigue that forced her to leave her supermarket cashier shift early yesterday. She typically lives alone in a small apartment, drives herself to work, and manages her own shopping and cooking without assistance. Past medical history is remarkable for stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing hypertensive nephrosclerosis—her outpatient nephrology note from two months ago documented a creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate in the mid-40s—but she has never required dialysis, has no record of myocardial infarction or pump dysfunction, and denies any malignancies, chronic liver conditions, cerebrovascular accidents, or residence in an institutional setting. Home medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily, chlorthalidone 25 mg every morning, and over-the-counter acetaminophen as needed; she does not take supplemental oxygen, inhalers, or diuretics. She quit smoking more than fifteen years earlier after a 10-pack-year exposure and drinks a single glass of wine on rare social occasions; illicit drug use is denied. On arrival she was seated upright on the stretcher, talking comfortably and answering questions appropriately with no confusion, naming the month, exact date, and location without hesitation. Initial vital signs recorded by triage personnel before any antipyretics, antibiotics, or intravenous fluids were administered showed an oral temperature of 37.4 °C, pulse 97 beats per minute regular, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg in the left arm, respiratory rate 21 breaths per minute with shallow sighing respirations, and oxygen saturation of 90 % on ambient air that rose to 93 % with 2 L/minute via nasal cannula. Physical examination revealed an alert, well-nourished female in mild respiratory distress only when talking in long sentences; mucous membranes were moist, sclerae anicteric, and neck supple without jugular venous distention. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a regular rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. The pulmonary exam showed decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower posterior lung field with fine inspiratory crackles just above that zone; whispered pectoriloquy was accentuated in the same region. There was no wheezing. Abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly was detected. Extremities were warm with brisk capillary refill, and no peripheral edema or clubbing was present. Neurologic screening demonstrated intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength, and normal heel-to-shin testing. Point-of-care laboratory data drawn prior to treatment included a finger-stick glucose of 108 mg/dL. Formal laboratories returned within the hour and revealed a hematocrit of 43 %, total leukocyte count 13.8 × 10⁹/L with 82 % neutrophils, serum sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 101 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 27 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.0 mg/dL—close to her baseline. A venous lactate measured 1.4 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas obtained while she remained on room air documented pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 70 mm Hg. An upright posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph demonstrated a dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with blunting of the right costophrenic angle and a small meniscus sign consistent with a modest pleural effusion; cardiac silhouette was normal in size, pulmonary vascularity unremarkable, and no ribs were fractured. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm at 95–100 beats per minute with nonspecific T-wave flattening in the lateral leads but no ischemic changes. Bedside lung ultrasound corroborated an anechoic stripe of fluid measuring approximately 8 mm adjacent to the diaphragm on the right and multiple static air bronchograms within the consolidated lobe. Urinalysis displayed 1+ protein without hematuria, congruent with her known renal impairment; there were no casts, nitrites, or leukocyte esterase. She reported producing similar volumes of urine at home and had voided after triage with amber-colored output. No antimicrobial agents, bronchodilators, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics had been administered before the completion of this examination and diagnostic workup in order to preserve baseline physiologic measurements.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points at presentation.
- Demographics: for a woman, age minus 10 gives 59 − 10 = 49. She lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: chronic renal disease adds 10. No malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: alert (no altered mental status), respiratory rate 21 (<30/min), systolic BP 122 (≥90 mm Hg), temperature 37.4 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 97 (<125/min) → 0 each.
- Laboratory findings: pH 7.40 (not <7.35), BUN 27 (not ≥30 mg/dL), sodium 139 (not <130 mEq/L), glucose 108 (not ≥250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 43% (not <30%) → 0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 70 mm Hg and saturation 90% meet neither hypoxemia cutoff (PaO₂ <60 or saturation <90%) → 0.
- Imaging: right pleural effusion → 10.
Total = 49 + 10 + 0 + 0 + 10 = 69.
Final answer: 69
